Newly settled California sheephead (Semicossyphus pulcher) emerge from the egg capsule as miniature, transparent larvae measuring just 0.20 centimeters [Lb = 0.20 centimeters] in total length at birth, a diminutive starting size typical of labrid fishes that produce pelagic eggs. During the first few days post-hatching, these endotrophic larvae rely entirely on their yolk reserves while undergoing rapid early development. At a water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the yolk-sac larva completes its transition to exogenous feeding after approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days], at which point mouth opening and first prey capture commence. This abbreviated lecithotrophic phase reflects the relatively small initial body size and the energetic demands of early growth in a warm-temperate marine environment. Following yolk absorption, the free-swimming larva enters a planktonic phase characterized by active feeding on copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton. The larval period is accompanied by progressive fin ray ossification and the development of the characteristic pigmentation patterns that distinguish juvenile S. pulcher from its congeneric relatives in the eastern Pacific.

Field surveys conducted across the Southern California Bight indicate that the standard length at puberty for California sheephead is 30.1 centimeters [Lp = 30.1 centimeters], a size typically attained between three and four years of age in this protogynous hermaphrodite. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 800 grams [Wwp = approximately 800 grams], representing a substantial increase from the larval stage and reflecting the allocation of resources toward somatic growth prior to the onset of reproductive function. Puberty in this species is marked by the initiation of gametogenesis and the development of the gonadal tissue that will eventually support the female phase of the life cycle. Individuals that reach this size threshold have generally recruited to rocky reef habitats and shifted from a diet of small invertebrates to one dominated by hard-shelled prey such as sea urchins and mollusks. The size at sexual maturation is notably larger than that observed in many other labrids, potentially reflecting the energetic costs associated with the specialized crushing dentition and jaw musculature required for durophagy.

Under laboratory conditions maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], comprehensive growth studies have revealed that the ultimate standard length for this species approaches 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], with the corresponding maximum recorded wet weight reaching 16,000 grams [Wwi = 16,000 grams]. These upper bounds represent the asymptotic size achieved by the largest individuals in the population, typically large, old females that have undergone the sex change characteristic of this protogynous species. The growth trajectory from juvenile to adult follows a decelerating curve, with the most rapid gains in length and mass occurring during the first decade of life before growth slows considerably as individuals approach their physiological maximum. Such large body sizes place S. pulcher among the largest labrids in the eastern Pacific, exceeded only by a few closely related species in the genus. The combination of a large ultimate body size and a long reproductive lifespan allows this species to exert significant top-down control on sea urchin populations, making it a keystone predator in kelp forest ecosystems.

At 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum daily reproductive output of California sheephead reaches approximately 85,000 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 85,000 eggs per day], a remarkably high fecundity that compensates for the substantial mortality experienced during the pelagic larval phase. This rate is derived from a production of approximately 1.94 million eggs per kilogram of body mass per year in females averaging 16 kilograms, with multiple spawning events occurring throughout the extended summer breeding period. The elevated fecundity reflects the species' strategy of producing large numbers of small, pelagic eggs that disperse widely via ocean currents, increasing the probability that at least some larvae will encounter suitable settlement habitat. This high reproductive potential is characteristic of many labrids and is a key factor in the species' ability to maintain population densities under moderate fishing pressure.

The maximum lifespan of California sheephead has been determined through otolith-based age estimation of specimens collected across its geographic range. At a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the oldest documented individuals reach approximately 53 years [am = approximately 53 years] of age, a longevity that places this species among the longer-lived labrids globally and reflects the slow somatic growth and late reproductive maturation characteristic of large-bodied reef fishes. The age at first reproduction occurs at approximately 1,460 days after hatching [tR = approximately 1,460 days after hatching], allowing individuals to contribute multiple decades of reproductive output, with fecundity increasing as body size at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]grows with age. This extended reproductive window is particularly significant given the species' protogynous sex change, as older, larger females eventually transform into males and continue breeding in the terminal sex. Such life-history traits have important implications for fisheries management, as the removal of large, old individuals can disproportionately reduce both reproductive output and the availability of spawning males within the population.
